The cross-sectional analysis included 7,635 young Australian women. The adjusted odds ratio for self-reported diagnosed anxiety per additional gram of estimated dietary oleic acid was 1.02 (95% CI 1.00–1.05, p=.046). The upper and lower bounds are rounded in the original. Estimates for non-diagnostic anxiety symptoms and the SF-36 mental-health measure were near null for oleic acid. The dietary model estimates a nutrient across foods, gives no pressing grade, and cannot assign these findings to olive oil or symptom severity in Parkinson disease.

The three-week active comparison randomized 23 women with fibromyalgia to organic extra-virgin olive oil (11) or refined olive oil (12). The reported between-group difference in pre-to-post SF-12 mental-component change is +11.228 points (95% robust CI 3.19–25.24, adjusted p=.035). The raw start values differ between groups and the pilot is small. The mental-component score is a composite, and the investigators do not report a separate anxiety estimate or a Parkinson cohort.

The incident ParkWest analysis included 212 cases and 175 matched controls. Table 2 gives habitual coffee of 3.37 versus 3.83 cups per day and a diagnosis odds ratio of 0.86 per additional cup in the reported regression (p=.007). The motor subtype coffee contrast was inconclusive (p=.09). The full report does not estimate fatigue by coffee consumption or distinguish the frozen brewing preparation. The later fatigue report shares the parent cohort while analyzing another question.
